deep.reconstruction:
Context: heliotrope era, c. 1821–23. Gauss invented the heliotrope in 1821, and the stations Hohehagen, Brocken and Inselsberg form his great triangle. The page holds four independent blocks.

(A) Time series, upper left. Gauss lists entries of the form date (April 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14), clock time (h.min, astronomical reckoning, e.g. 22.40), value. The values run −6.8, −7.2, −7.7 | −8.7, −8.95 | −10.95, −11.07, −11.25, −11.70 | −14.00, −14.50, −15.25 | 17.25, 17.50, 18.50, 18.75 | 34.40 (Apr 14, 4h30).
- From 17.25 on the minus sign is evidently just omitted, since the values continue monotonically.
- The quantity grows by roughly 2.5–3 units per day, faster towards the end. It is most plausibly a chronometer or clock correction in seconds (my conjecture; nothing on the page names it).

(A') Interpolation table, upper right. It gives values at decimal-hour epochs:
- Apr 7, 6.92h: −7.23
- Apr 8, 0.58h: −8.82
- Apr 9, 1.77h: −11.24
- Apr 10, 2.82h: −14.58
- Apr 11, 1.98h: −18.00
These are linear interpolations in table A (my check). For example, Apr 8 0.58h lies between Apr 7 22h40 (−8.7) and Apr 8 2h30 (−8.95), giving −8.825. Apr 11 1.98h lies between Apr 10 22h50 (17.50) and Apr 11 5h15 (18.50), giving 17.99. The epochs are presumably the times of heliotrope or other observations.

(B) 'Sterngrössen' (star magnitudes). Magnitude m = 1…7 is mapped to the brightness ratio
- 1, 2.3, 5.4, 12.4, 28.6, 66.2, 153.1 (magnitude 8 left blank).
- This is a geometric scale I(1)/I(m) = q^(m−1) with q = 153.1^(1/6) ≈ 2.313.
- That q reproduces every entry to the last digit: q² = 5.35, q³ = 12.37, q⁴ = 28.62, q⁵ = 66.2. So it is a fixed-ratio magnitude scale with ratio about 2.31 per magnitude (log10 q ≈ 0.364).

(C) Mirror area. 'Die Dimensionen des Spiegels am ersten Heliotrop sind 35.6 mm × 53.5 mm' = 1904.6 mm².

(D) Heliotrope brightness at distance Δ. Gauss states
- H(Δ) = (619300 m/Δ)² · (0.1)^(Δ/84467 m).
- The unit is Aldebaran seen by day at the same altitude as the illuminating Sun.
- The first factor is the inverse-square law. 619300 m is the distance at which the heliotrope would equal Aldebaran without atmospheric loss.
- The second factor is exponential (Bouguer–Lambert) atmospheric extinction: transmission drops by a factor 10 every 84467 m, i.e. about 2.7 %/km, or about 0.030 mag/km.
- A note states the formula assumes a mirror area of 221 mm², with no allowance for weakening by the foil (silvering) or for inclination.

In logs, log10 H = 2(log 619300 − log Δ) − 10^(log Δ − log 84467). Gauss uses log 619300 = 5.79190 and log 84467 = 4.92669 throughout.
- Hohehagen–Brocken: log Δ = 4.83997 (Δ ≈ 69,176 m). Then 5.79190 − 4.83997 = 0.95193, ×2 = 1.90386. The extinction exponent is 10^(4.83997 − 4.92669) = 0.81900. So log H = 1.08486 and H = 12.16.
- Hohehagen–Sternwarte Göttingen (column headed 'Hoheh.–Sternw.'): log Δ = 4.13992 (Δ ≈ 13,800 m). Then 1.65198, ×2 = 3.30396. The exponent is 0.16339. So log H = 3.14057 and H = 1382.2.
- Hohehagen–Inselsberg: log Δ = 5.02520 (Δ ≈ 105,975 m). Then 0.76670, ×2 = 1.53340. The exponent is 10^0.09851 = 1.25462. So log H = 0.27878 and H = 1.900 (the '1.900' at bottom right is this result).

Thus a 221 mm² heliotrope would appear about 12 times as bright as daytime Aldebaran on the Brocken line and about 1.9 times on the Inselsberg line. The real mirror (1904.6 mm², about 8.6 × 221) would give correspondingly more, before losses.

[My consistency check, not on the page.] A flat mirror of area A reflecting the Sun gives illuminance E_sun·A/(Ω_sun·d²), with Ω_sun ≈ 6.80e-5 sr. Gauss's constant then implies E_sun/E_Ald = A/(Ω_sun·619300²) inverted, about 1.18e11, i.e. 27.7 mag. The modern value is about 27.6 mag (−26.74 vs +0.85), so the 619300 m constant is physically very reasonable.
errors: Table A: from Apr 10 21h35 onward the minus signs are omitted (17.25 … 34.40 should read −17.25 … −34.40); an omission, not a computational error.

Table A': two of the interpolated values do not follow from linear interpolation in table A as read. Apr 9 1.77h gives about −11.14, not −11.24. Apr 10 2.82h (≈ the tabulated 2h50 = −14.50) gives about −14.50, not −14.58. Either a different time argument or reduction is involved, or these are slips of about 0.1.
Heliotrope computations (Brocken, Sternwarte, Inselsberg) check to all digits given. log10 619300 = 5.79190 and log10 84467 = 4.92669 are correct.
The magnitude ratios are internally consistent with q ≈ 2.313. The entry 2.3 is q rounded, while 5.4 is q² (5.35) rounded upward, so the table was computed from q, not from 2.3.
The cancelled first attempt at the Inselsberg exponent (overwritten as 1.25462) and the struck line below it are self-corrections, not surviving errors.

results.what: Brightness of a heliotrope at distance Δ = inverse-square factor times exponential atmospheric extinction, H = (619300/Δ)^2 · 0.1^(Δ/84467), in units of daytime Aldebaran; evaluated for Hohehagen–Brocken (12.16), Hohehagen–Göttingen observatory (1382.2), Hohehagen–Inselsberg (1.900)
results.modern_name: Inverse-square law combined with Bouguer–Lambert(–Beer) extinction law (horizontal atmospheric transmission)

results.what: Geometric magnitude scale with fixed ratio ≈ 2.313 per magnitude (1, 2.3, 5.4, 12.4, 28.6, 66.2, 153.1 for magnitudes 1–7)
results.usually_credited_to: Pogson (1856, ratio 2.512); earlier photometric ratio estimates by J. Herschel and Steinheil (1830s)

results.what: Area of the first heliotrope mirror 35.6 mm × 53.5 mm = 1904.6 mm²
Linear interpolation of a time series (probably clock corrections) to observation epochs

deep.surprise_reason: The arithmetic and the extinction law are standard for the period, and Gauss's photometric interest in the heliotrope is known. Two things are notable. First, there is an explicit quantitative photometric model of heliotrope visibility: inverse square plus exponential extinction, calibrated to daytime Aldebaran, with a constant that agrees with the modern Sun/Aldebaran ratio. Second, there is a fixed-ratio (≈2.31) geometric magnitude scale written down c. 1821–23, decades before Pogson. Such a ratio scale was not unheard of before Pogson, and I am unsure whether this note is already published (e.g. in Werke IX). So it is a notable unpublished detail rather than a major priority claim.

checkable.asserts: implied Aldebaran/Sun illuminance ratio ≈ 8.5e-12 (≈27.7 mag), close to modern 27.6 mag (my check, not on page)

transcription_corrections: Column heading 'Hoheh. − Insel[?]' should read 'Hoheh. − Sternw.' (Hohehagen–Sternwarte Göttingen, log Δ = 4.13992, Δ ≈ 13.8 km). The Inselsberg computation is the right-hand column with log Δ = 5.02520.
The small struck entry under 4.13992 is a cancelled '4.92669' (log 84467), not '4.92667'.

'1.[-25462-]' is the overwritten/corrected value 1.25462, which is retained, followed by a struck-out line. '1.900' (bottom right) is the result of the Inselsberg computation, not part of the sentence about the formula.
Values 17,25, 17,50, 18,50, 18,75, 34,40 and 18,00 lack the minus sign in the manuscript but continue the negative series.
In table A the '9' before 1.30 and 2.10 is a day number written in the margin (written twice, once overwritten).
Sentence probably reads: 'wo der Aldebaran, bei Tage, in der Höhe, worin zugleich die beleuchtende ☉ steht, als Einheit angenommen.'
'am ersten Heliotrop' may be 'zum ersten Heliotrop'; the closing note is 'ohne Rücksicht auf Folieschwächung u. Neigung'.
